questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is a parody about handing your data to a stranger over a laggy network. Who wrote it, and in what piece?

options.text: Kyle Kingsbury, Carly Rae Jepsen and the Perils of Network Partitions
Leslie Lamport, Time, Clocks and the Ordering of Events (1978)
Coda Hale, You Can't Sacrifice Partition Tolerance (2010)
Eric Brewer, CAP Twelve Years Later (2012)

questions.explanation: 'Hope' is the operative word — in an asynchronous network you cannot know whether the write landed.

questions.question: Which prior discussions does the opening name as examples of handling things going wrong? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Replica failover, under Handling Node Outages
Replication lag, under Problems with Replication Lag
Concurrency control for transactions, under Weak Isolation Levels
Schema evolution, covered under Modes of Dataflow in Chapter 4

questions.explanation: As we come to understand various edge cases that can occur in real systems, we get better at handling them.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about the honesty of the previous chapters, and what assumption does it adopt?

options.text: That the earlier chapters were still too optimistic; the reality is darker
The previous chapters were too pessimistic; this one assumes faults are rare
The previous chapters were accurate; this one adds only clock issues
The previous chapters ignored faults entirely

questions.explanation: A footnote carves out one exception: faults are assumed to be non-Byzantine, meaning nodes do not lie.

questions.question: What does the chapter name as the main difference between distributed systems and single-computer software?

options.text: That there are lots of new and exciting ways for things to go wrong
That performance becomes considerably harder to predict
That the codebase grows larger and harder to test properly
That all data must be serialized before it can be sent

questions.explanation: The goal is a taste of the problems that arise in practice, and an understanding of the things we can and cannot rely on.

questions.question: How does the opening define the engineer's task?

options.text: To build systems that do their job despite everything going wrong
To eliminate every possible fault from the system design
To detect faults as quickly as they can possibly be detected
To document every failure mode before the system is built

questions.explanation: Guarantees despite faults, not absence of faults.

questions.question: Which problem areas does the opening preview, in order?

options.text: Unreliable networks, unreliable clocks, and knowledge, truth and lies
Replication, partitioning and distributed transactions
Consensus, total ordering and atomic commit protocols
Batch processing, stream processing and the future of data systems

questions.explanation: The chapter says the consequences of all these issues are disorienting, and describes itself as a thoroughly pessimistic and depressing overview of things that may go wrong, giving a bleak outlook.

questions.question: How does the chapter characterize a program running on a single computer?

options.text: Predictably: either it works or it doesn't, rarely something in between
Unpredictably, because of variability in the underlying hardware
Predictably, but only while the machine is under light load
It always fails partially, exactly as a distributed system does

questions.explanation: There is no fundamental reason why software on a single computer should be flaky: when the hardware is working correctly, the same operation always produces the same result — it is deterministic.

questions.question: When a single computer does have a hardware problem, what is the usual consequence?

options.text: Total failure — a kernel panic, a blue screen, or a failure to boot
Partial degradation, in which wrong results are returned to callers
Silent data corruption that produces no visible symptom at all
Reduced throughput, while operation remains entirely correct

questions.explanation: Examples given include a kernel panic, a blue screen of death, failure to start up, and memory corruption from a loose connector.

questions.question: Why is the all-or-nothing behaviour of a computer described as deliberate?

options.text: Because a wrong result is harder to handle than an outright crash
Because crashing is cheaper to implement than error recovery
Because operating systems cannot detect partial faults
The behaviour is not deliberate at all; it is an accident of hardware design

questions.explanation: Escalating partial failure into total failure is a design choice made to keep results trustworthy.

questions.question: What do computers hide, and how far back does the chapter trace this design goal?

options.text: They present an idealized model that operates with mathematical perfection
They hide network latency, and the goal dates from the 1970s
They hide concurrency, and the goal dates from the 1990s
They hide nothing at all; the physical reality is fully exposed

questions.explanation: The idealized model is what distributed systems cannot sustain.

questions.question: The Coda Hale anecdote lists failures from one operator's 'limited experience'. Which does it include? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Network partitions in a single datacenter, PDU failures and switch failures
Accidental power cycles of whole racks, whole-datacenter backbone failures and whole-datacenter power failures
A hypoglycemic driver smashing his Ford pickup truck into a datacenter's HVAC system
A software bug in the database engine that returns wrong results

questions.explanation: And he adds 'I'm not even an ops guy' — in the physical world, a remarkably wide range of things can go wrong.

questions.question: Define partial failure, and say what makes it difficult.

options.text: Partial failure: some parts broken while others work, unpredictably
Partial failure means half the nodes are down; the difficulty is capacity
Partial failure means data is partially written; the difficulty is corruption
Partial failure means slow responses; the difficulty is latency

questions.explanation: This nondeterminism and possibility of partial failures is what makes distributed systems hard to work with.

questions.question: Match the philosophies in the 'Cloud Computing and Supercomputing' box. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High-performance computing: supercomputers with thousands of CPUs, typically used for computationally intensive scientific computing tasks such as weather forecasting or molecular dynamics
Cloud computing: often associated with multi-tenant datacenters, commodity computers connected with an IP network (often Ethernet), elastic/on-demand resource allocation, and metered billing
Traditional enterprise datacenters lie somewhere between these extremes
Cloud computing is a precisely defined technical term with an agreed meaning

questions.explanation: Note the honesty of the middle definition: cloud computing is not a well-defined term, so the chapter describes it by association.

questions.question: How does a supercomputer handle a fault?

options.text: Checkpoint to durable storage and restart the whole job on failure
It routes around the failed node automatically with no interruption
It replicates all state, so no checkpoint is needed
It ignores the failure and continues with degraded results

questions.explanation: The supercomputer model is deliberately the opposite of the cloud model.

questions.question: State the online/offline contrast between internet services and supercomputers.

options.text: Because online services must serve users with low latency at any time
Both are online services that cannot tolerate any downtime
Both are offline batch jobs that can be restarted freely
Internet services are offline batch jobs; supercomputers are online

questions.explanation: Availability requirements are what rule out stop-and-repair for internet services.

questions.question: Contrast supercomputer and cloud nodes on hardware and communication.

options.text: Specialized reliable hardware, with shared memory and remote direct memory access
Both are built from commodity hardware and communicate by message passing
Both are built from specialized hardware and communicate by shared memory
Supercomputers use commodity hardware while cloud services use specialized

questions.explanation: Reliable specialized nodes with shared memory versus unreliable commodity nodes with messages.

questions.question: Which network topologies does the chapter attribute to each, and why?

options.text: IP and Ethernet in Clos topologies, versus specialized supercomputer topologies
Both use Clos topologies chosen for high bisection bandwidth
Both use meshes and toruses suited to known communication patterns
Datacenters use toruses while supercomputers are built on Ethernet

questions.explanation: Known communication patterns is what makes a specialized topology pay for HPC.

questions.question: What does scale do to the probability of brokenness, and what does that cost the give-up-and-restart strategy?

options.text: The bigger the system, the likelier that some component is always broken
Scale reduces the probability of brokenness, because of redundancy
Scale has no effect on the probability that something is broken
Scale makes the give-up-and-restart approach cheaper than repair

questions.explanation: 'Something is always broken' is the working assumption at scale.

questions.question: What operational benefits follow from tolerating failed nodes? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Rolling upgrade: restarting one node at a time, while the service continues serving users without interruption
In a cloud environment, if one virtual machine is not performing well, you can just kill it and request a new one, hoping that the new one will be faster
Faults become impossible once the job is checkpointed to storage
Checkpointing becomes unnecessary, because the state is never lost

questions.explanation: Both convert node-level disposability into operational freedom.

questions.question: Why does geographic distribution make things worse?

options.text: Because communication most likely goes over the internet
Because clocks cannot be synchronized across distance
Because data cannot be replicated across regions
It does not make things worse

questions.explanation: The internet as the interconnect is the qualitative change.

questions.question: State the chapter's mandate for making distributed systems work, and its caveat.

options.text: Accept partial failure and build fault tolerance into the software
We must eliminate partial failure through better hardware
We must accept that distributed systems cannot be reliable
We must use supercomputer-style checkpointing

questions.explanation: Reliability from unreliability, with an honest ceiling.

questions.question: Why must even a small system think about partial failure? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because it is important to consider a wide range of possible faults — even fairly unlikely ones — and to artificially create such situations in your testing environment to see what happens; in distributed systems, suspicion, pessimism, and paranoia pay off

Because in a distributed system, even if most of the components are working correctly most of the time, sooner or later some part of the system will become faulty, so fault handling must be part of the software design
Because you, as operator of the software, need to know what behavior to expect from the software in the case of a fault
Because it is wise to assume that faults are rare and simply hope for the best when they occur

questions.explanation: The last statement is exactly what the chapter says is unwise.

questions.question: The 'Building a Reliable System from Unreliable Components' box names an intuition and rejects it. Which?

options.text: That a system is only as reliable as its least reliable component
That adding redundancy always improves overall reliability
That reliability is directly proportional to money spent
That software can never be more reliable than its hardware

questions.explanation: The whole box exists to contradict the weakest-link intuition.

questions.question: Which unreliability does each box example mask, and what are their limits? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Error-correcting codes allow digital data to be transmitted accurately across a communication channel that occasionally gets some bits wrong, for example due to radio interference on a wireless network

IP is unreliable — it may drop, delay, duplicate, or reorder packets — but TCP provides a more reliable transport layer on top: missing packets are retransmitted, duplicates are eliminated, and packets are reassembled into the order in which they were sent

Error correction can handle a small number of single-bit errors, but if your signal is swamped by interference there is a fundamental limit to how much data you can get through your communication channel
TCP can hide packet loss and reordering, and its retransmission removes variable network delay as well

questions.explanation: TCP cannot remove delay — it can hide packet loss, duplication and reordering, but not the time the network takes. Note which of IP's four sins TCP does not fix: delay. That omission is the seed of the entire unreliable-networks discussion.

questions.question: If the higher-level system is not perfect, why bother with a leaky abstraction?

options.text: Because it makes the remaining faults easier to reason about
Because a leaky abstraction is always better than none
Because the abstraction can be made perfect with enough effort
You shouldn't bother; leaky abstractions should be removed

questions.explanation: Fewer and simpler remaining faults is the payoff, not their elimination.

questions.question: What kind of systems does Part II focus on, and what does the architecture forbid?

options.text: Shared-nothing: machines with private memory, communicating only by network
Shared-disk systems, in which every machine reaches one storage array
Shared-memory systems, communicating by remote direct memory access
Single-machine systems, in which there is no network at all

questions.explanation: Shared-nothing became dominant for internet services because it is comparatively cheap, requiring no special hardware; it can make use of commoditized cloud computing services; and it can achieve high reliability through redundancy across multiple geographically distributed datacenters.

questions.question: Define an asynchronous packet network.

options.text: Asynchronous packet networks, with no guarantee of arrival or timing
A network with bounded delay and guaranteed message delivery
A network in which messages are always delivered in order
A circuit-switched network with bandwidth reserved per connection

questions.explanation: No timing guarantee and no delivery guarantee — both matter.

questions.question: You send a request and expect a response. Which failures are possible? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Your request may have been lost, perhaps someone unplugged a network cable; or it may be waiting in a queue and will be delivered later, perhaps the network or the recipient is overloaded

The remote node may have failed, perhaps it crashed or was powered down; or it may have temporarily stopped responding, perhaps because of a long garbage collection pause, but will start responding again later
The remote node may have processed the request and sent a response which arrives corrupted and is silently accepted
The remote node may have processed your request, but the response has been delayed and will be delivered later, perhaps the network or your own machine is overloaded

questions.explanation: Silent acceptance of corruption is not on the list; checksums normally catch it. The genuine case is that the response is lost on the network, for example to a network switch misconfiguration. Six possibilities. Note the last one includes your own machine as a possible cause.

questions.question: Why can't the sender simply check whether its packet was delivered?

options.text: Because the sender cannot tell whether the packet was delivered
Because the network protocol has no support for acknowledgments
Because the sender's clock may be wrong about the send time
It can tell — TCP acknowledgments already provide exactly this

questions.explanation: Figure 8-1 shows that if you send a request and don't get a response, it's not possible to distinguish whether the request was lost, the remote node is down, or the response was lost.

questions.question: What does a timeout tell you, and what residual uncertainty remains?

options.text: You give up waiting, still not knowing whether the request arrived
It tells you definitively that the remote node has died
It tells you the request was definitely not processed
It tells you the response was lost rather than the request

questions.explanation: A timeout is a decision, not information.

questions.question: What did the study of a medium-sized datacenter find?

options.text: About 12 faults per month, half per-machine and half per-rack
About 2 network faults per year, all of them at rack level
About 100 faults per month, all of them single-machine
Effectively none, which is why the study was published

questions.explanation: 12 per month is roughly 144 per year, split 72/72 between single-machine and rack-level.

questions.question: Does redundant networking gear help as much as you might hope?

options.text: No — redundancy reduced faults less than expected
Yes, redundancy eliminates network faults entirely
Yes, redundancy reduces faults proportionally to the number of paths
The study found redundancy increases faults

questions.explanation: Human error is the failure mode redundancy does not address.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about public cloud versus private datacenter networks?

options.text: EC2 is notorious for transient glitches; private datacenters can be stable
Private datacenter networks experience no network faults at all
EC2 turns out to be more reliable than a private datacenter
The two are equally unreliable, with no measurable difference

questions.explanation: A real difference in degree, but not in kind.

questions.question: What surprising fault involving a network interface does the chapter describe?

options.text: An interface that dropped all inbound packets but sent outbound ones fine
An interface that silently duplicated every packet it sent
An interface that reordered packets but never dropped one
An interface that corrupted inbound packets but not outbound

questions.explanation: Asymmetric connectivity is what makes failure detection especially treacherous — picked up again under The Truth Is Defined by the Majority. The chapter also notes that sharks might bite undersea cables and damage them.

questions.question: What terminology does the 'Network partitions' box settle on, and why?

options.text: A network partition, or netsplit
It prefers 'netsplit' to avoid confusion with CAP
It prefers 'network partition' as the standard term
It uses all three terms interchangeably

questions.explanation: Avoiding collision with Chapter 6's sense of 'partition' is the reason.

questions.question: Which disasters does the chapter name for software meeting an untested network fault? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The cluster could become deadlocked and permanently unable to serve requests, even when the network recovers
It could delete all of your data
It could silently corrupt only the most recent writes
It could duplicate every write exactly once on recovery

questions.explanation: If software is put in an unanticipated situation it may do arbitrary unexpected things. The second example is cited from an analysis of Redis Sentinel properties and failure scenarios.

questions.question: Distinguish handling network faults from tolerating them.

options.text: No — showing users an error message can be a valid response
They are the same thing under two different names
Tolerating means showing an error; handling means full recovery
Neither is necessary when the network is normally reliable

questions.explanation: Knowing the reaction is mandatory; masking the fault is optional.

questions.question: Why is automatic detection of faulty nodes needed? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A load balancer needs to stop sending requests to a node that is dead — take it out of rotation
In a distributed database with single-leader replication, if the leader fails, one of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader
To recompute the entire replication log from scratch
To synchronize the clocks across the whole cluster

questions.explanation: Both require a verdict on liveness, which the network cannot supply reliably.

questions.question: What explicit feedback do you get when no process is listening on the destination port, and what does it fail to tell you?

options.text: The operating system closes or refuses the connection with RST or FIN
You receive an ICMP echo reply confirming it was processed
You receive nothing at all, so a timeout is your only signal
You receive a full transaction log of what was processed

questions.explanation: Connection-level feedback says nothing about application-level progress. A second mechanism: if a node process crashed but the operating system is still running, a script can notify other nodes about the crash so another node can take over without waiting for a timeout to expire — HBase does this.

questions.question: You can query switch management interfaces to detect link failures. When is that option ruled out? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you're connecting via the internet
If you're in a shared datacenter with no access to the switches themselves
If you can't reach the management interface due to a network problem
If the remote machine is powered down, since a powered-down machine cannot be distinguished from a healthy one

questions.explanation: A powered-down machine is exactly the case switch management interfaces can report on. The listed obstacles are the internet, a shared datacenter with no switch access, and being unable to reach the management interface itself. The last case is subtle: hardware-level link detection rules out network faults but cannot distinguish a crash from a power-down that also killed the link.

questions.question: What does a router send when it is sure an address is unreachable, and what limitation applies?

options.text: An ICMP Destination Unreachable packet
An ICMP echo request, which is fully reliable
A TCP RST, which is definitive
Nothing at all, because routers never report unreachability

questions.explanation: The router's knowledge is as partial as anyone else's.

questions.question: What is the chapter's rule about knowing a request succeeded?

options.text: A positive response from the application itself
A TCP acknowledgment from the remote host is sufficient
The absence of an error response is sufficient evidence
A timeout that has not yet expired is sufficient evidence

questions.explanation: Rapid feedback about a remote node being down is useful but you can't count on it. The general procedure: you may get an error response at some level of the stack, but in general you have to assume that you will get no response at all — you can retry a few times, wait for a timeout to elapse, and eventually declare the node dead.

questions.question: How long should a timeout be? State the trade-off.

options.text: There is unfortunately no simple answer
Always use 30 seconds, the standard value
Always use the shortest possible timeout
Always use the longest tolerable timeout

questions.explanation: Detection latency versus false positives, with no universally right point.

questions.question: Why is prematurely declaring a node dead problematic?

options.text: Because the node may be alive and midway through an action
Because the node's data will be deleted when it is declared dead
Because the node will not be able to rejoin the cluster afterwards
Because the clocks on the two nodes will drift further apart

questions.explanation: Duplicated side effects are the concrete harm; the chapter points forward to Chapters 9 and 11.

questions.question: Explain the cascading failure mechanism from premature timeouts.

options.text: Extra load on the remaining nodes, which can cascade into more failures
Premature timeouts reduce load, by shedding work early
Premature timeouts affect only the node that timed out
Cascading failure comes from long timeouts, not short ones

questions.explanation: Load transfer under overload is a positive feedback loop.

questions.question: In the fictitious system with bounded delays, what timeout follows — and for d = 20 ms and r = 100 ms, what is it?

options.text: That delay is bounded by d and handling time by r
A total of d + r, which works out to 120 ms
A total of 2(d + r), which works out to 240 ms
A total of d + 2r, which works out to 220 ms

questions.explanation: Two network traversals plus one handling time.

questions.question: Why is 2d + r unavailable in reality?

options.text: Both fail: delays are unbounded and nodes can pause arbitrarily
Only the network assumption fails; response times are bounded
Only the response-time assumption fails; networks are bounded
Neither assumption fails, which is why 2d + r is used in practice

questions.explanation: Unbounded on both axes, and 'fast most of the time' is not the same as bounded.

questions.question: What analogy opens 'Network congestion and queueing', and what is the dominant cause of packet-delay variability?

options.text: Traffic congestion on road networks
The analogy is air traffic control; the cause is routing changes
The analogy is postal delivery; the cause is packet loss
The analogy is water pipes; the cause is bandwidth limits

questions.explanation: Queueing, not distance or bandwidth, dominates delay variability.

questions.question: Which sources of queueing does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the network switch: if several different nodes simultaneously try to send packets to the same destination, the switch must queue them up and feed them into the destination network link one by one, so a packet may have to wait a while until it can get a slot — this is network congestion. If the switch queue fills up, the packet is dropped, so it has to be resent even though the network is functioning fine

At the destination machine: when a packet reaches the destination machine, if all CPU cores are currently busy, the incoming request from the network is queued by the operating system until the application is ready to handle it, which may take an arbitrary length of time

In virtualized environments: a running operating system is often paused for tens of milliseconds while another virtual machine uses a CPU core. During this time the VM cannot consume any data from the network, so incoming data is queued (buffered) by the virtual machine monitor, further increasing the variability of network delays
At the sender: TCP flow control eliminates queueing altogether by refusing to send until the network is completely idle

questions.explanation: Flow control (also called congestion avoidance or backpressure) limits a node's own send rate rather than waiting for an idle network — and it moves the queueing into the sender. Four sources, at the switch, the destination CPU, the hypervisor and the sender.

questions.question: How does TCP decide a packet is lost, and what does the application observe?

options.text: It retransmits after a timeout derived from observed round-trip times
TCP never retransmits, so the application must handle the loss
The application sees the loss itself, though not the delay
TCP retransmits immediately, without waiting for any timeout

questions.explanation: Two waits, serially — which is exactly the delay TCP cannot magically remove.

questions.question: What does the 'TCP Versus UDP' box say about UDP?

options.text: UDP, used by videoconferencing and Voice over IP
UDP eliminates all delay variability
UDP performs flow control but not retransmission
UDP is more reliable than TCP

questions.explanation: Dropping reliability reduces some sources of delay but not queueing or scheduling.

questions.question: Why is retransmission pointless in a VoIP call?

options.text: Because retransmitting data that is already too late is pointless
Because UDP forbids retransmission at the protocol level
Because audio packets are too large to be retransmitted
Because voice data is not sensitive to errors in the first place

questions.explanation: The deadline, not the protocol, is what makes retransmission worthless.

questions.question: Why do queueing delays have an especially wide range near maximum capacity?

options.text: Because spare capacity lets queues drain before they build up
Because switches drop more packets at low utilization
Because TCP disables flow control near capacity
Because CPU scheduling becomes deterministic near capacity

questions.explanation: Queue growth is nonlinear in utilization, which is why tail latency explodes near saturation.

questions.question: In multi-tenant environments, what is shared and what term describes the offender?

options.text: No insight into other tenants' use of the shared links and machines
Only the network links are shared, and the effect is called congestion
Only the CPUs are shared, and the effect is called steal time
Nothing is genuinely shared between tenants in a public cloud

questions.explanation: Links, switches, interfaces and CPUs all shared — hence unpredictable delays.

questions.question: What measurement procedure does the chapter prescribe for choosing timeouts?

options.text: Measure round-trip times over time and derive the timeout from them
Use the maximum round-trip time observed on a single machine
Use whatever default value the database vendor recommends
Use the median of a one-minute sample of round-trip times

questions.explanation: Measured distribution, not a guessed constant.

questions.question: What does the chapter recommend instead of constant timeouts, and which systems use it?

options.text: Continually measure jitter and adjust timeouts automatically
A fixed exponential backoff, as used in HBase and Kafka
A fixed 30-second timeout, as used by ZooKeeper sessions
No timeout at all, as used by Riak's request handling

questions.explanation: Adaptive timeouts driven by measured jitter.

questions.question: Which comparison case does the chapter reach for when asking why networks can't just be made reliable?

options.text: The traditional fixed-line telephone network
The postal system, which guarantees delivery
The electrical grid, which guarantees voltage
The air traffic control network

questions.explanation: A network that does deliver bounded latency, which invites the question of why datacenters can't.

questions.question: Describe a telephone circuit and the ISDN numbers.

options.text: A circuit, with a fixed guaranteed bandwidth reserved end to end
8,000 frames per second with 8 bits each, giving 64,000 bits per second
4,000 frames per second with 8 bits each, giving 32,000 bits per second
1,000 frames per second with 64 bits each

questions.explanation: 4,000 frames per second is one frame every 250 microseconds; 4,000 times 16 bits is 64,000 bits per second.

questions.question: Why does a circuit give bounded delay?

options.text: Because reserved space per hop removes queueing entirely
Because circuit routers are faster than packet routers
Because the circuit uses UDP in place of TCP framing
Because the volume of audio data is small enough to fit

questions.explanation: Pre-reserved capacity at every hop is what eliminates queueing.

questions.question: Contrast a telephone circuit with a TCP connection.

options.text: A circuit reserves bandwidth nobody else can use; TCP shares it opportunistically
Both reserve bandwidth; a TCP connection simply reserves less of it
Both are opportunistic; the circuit merely gets scheduling priority
A TCP connection reserves its bandwidth even while sitting idle

questions.explanation: Reservation versus opportunism is the whole difference.

questions.question: Why can't Ethernet and IP promise a maximum round-trip time?

options.text: Because packet switching brings queueing and so unbounded delays
Because Ethernet is too slow to carry reserved circuits
Because the IP protocol is stateless between packets
They can do so, but implementations choose not to enable it

questions.explanation: No circuit means no reservation means queueing means unbounded delay.

questions.question: Which hybrid attempts does the chapter cite, and what does InfiniBand do?

options.text: Hybrids such as ATM, with InfiniBand having some similarities
Only MPLS, since InfiniBand is purely a storage protocol
Only Token Ring, since InfiniBand implements circuit switching
No such hybrid protocols have ever been built or deployed

questions.explanation: Link-layer flow control reduces but does not eliminate queueing.

questions.question: How can circuits be emulated on packet networks?

options.text: Quality of service and admission control
By disabling TCP flow control
By reserving IP addresses per flow
Circuits cannot be emulated on packet networks

questions.explanation: Note 'statistically bounded' — not the same as bounded.

questions.question: Work through the 'Latency and Resource Utilization' box's 10,000-call wire example.

options.text: A fixed number of call slots, each occupied for the call's duration
All 10,000 slots are shared dynamically, giving no guarantee
The wire adapts its capacity to the number of calls
Unused slots are reallocated to active calls

questions.explanation: Static partitioning buys guarantees and wastes capacity.

questions.question: How does the internet allocate bandwidth, and what is the upside of the resulting queueing?

options.text: It shares bandwidth dynamically, with senders jostling for the wire
It reserves bandwidth per flow, with no queueing and no cost benefit
It allocates capacity round-robin, which bounds the delay
It does not allocate bandwidth between senders at all

questions.explanation: Cheaper bytes is the payoff for accepting variable delay.

questions.question: How does the box carry the argument over to CPUs?

options.text: CPU cores shared dynamically between threads
CPUs are always statically partitioned, unlike networks
CPU scheduling has no effect on latency
The argument does not carry over to CPUs

questions.explanation: The same utilization-versus-predictability trade-off, one layer down.

questions.question: State the box's closing verdict.

options.text: Only where resources are statically partitioned
Variable delays are a law of nature and cannot be avoided
Static partitioning is always cheaper
Dynamic partitioning gives both low cost and bounded delay

questions.explanation: 'Not a law of nature, but a cost/benefit trade-off' is the line to remember.

questions.question: Where does the chapter say quality of service is currently not enabled?

options.text: In multi-tenant datacenters, public clouds, and over the internet
Only inside private datacenters that you own outright
Only on wireless networks, where interference dominates
Quality of service is enabled everywhere by default today

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that peering agreements between internet service providers and the establishment of routes through the Border Gateway Protocol bear closer resemblance to circuit switching than IP itself — at that level it is possible to buy dedicated bandwidth, but internet routing operates at the level of networks, not individual connections between hosts, and at a much longer timescale.

questions.question: True or false: an asynchronous network has bounded delay; a synchronous network avoids queueing because bandwidth is reserved at every hop; TCP turns an unbounded-delay network into a bounded-delay one; statistically bounded delay is the same as bounded delay.

options.text: False, true, false, false
True, true, true, true
False, false, true, true
True, false, false, true

questions.explanation: Only the synchronous-network claim is true as stated.

questions.question: Which questions does the chapter list that applications use clocks to answer? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Has this request timed out yet? What's the 99th percentile response time of this service?
How many queries per second did this service handle on average in the last five minutes? How long did the user spend on our site?
When was this article published? At what date and time should the reminder email be sent? — both answered with a monotonic clock
When does this cache entry expire? What is the timestamp on this error message in the log file?

questions.explanation: Those are time-of-day questions, which need a wall-clock rather than a monotonic clock. Both kinds of question appear in the chapter's list; the distinction is which clock answers them. Eight questions in all: the first four measure durations, the last four describe points in time.

questions.question: What is the core reason time is tricky in a distributed system?

options.text: Because a message takes time to cross the network
Because clocks are cheap and therefore inaccurate
Because time zones differ between machines
Because leap seconds are unpredictable

questions.explanation: Unknown, variable message delay is what breaks ordering by timestamp.

questions.question: What physical device is a machine's clock, and what is the standard synchronization mechanism?

options.text: A quartz crystal oscillator, which is not perfectly accurate
An atomic clock, synchronized by GPS directly
A software counter, synchronized by the operating system
A network timestamp, with no local device

questions.explanation: Note it is a group of servers, which is what allows outlier rejection.

questions.question: Define the time-of-day clock precisely.

options.text: The current date and time by some calendar — wall-clock time
It returns nanoseconds since the computer was started
It returns a monotonically increasing counter with no calendar meaning
It returns seconds since the year 2000 including leap seconds

questions.explanation: A footnote clarifies that although the clock is called real-time, it has nothing to do with real-time operating systems.

questions.question: Why can't time-of-day clocks measure elapsed time? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Backward jumps: if the local clock is too far ahead of the NTP server, it may be forcibly reset and appear to jump back to a previous point in time
Leap seconds: they often ignore leap seconds, which makes the timeline inconsistent
They have coarse-grained resolution — for example moving forward only in steps of 10 ms on older Windows systems
They cannot be synchronized with one another at all

questions.explanation: The jumps and leap-second handling make them unsuitable for measuring elapsed time; the resolution problem is less of a problem on recent systems. Time-of-day clocks are usually synchronized with NTP, which means a timestamp from one machine ideally means the same as on another.

questions.question: Define the monotonic clock and explain its name.

options.text: Measuring a duration or interval, such as a timeout
It returns calendar time and is named for its monotone units
It is named for being monotonic in frequency, not in value
It always moves backward on resynchronization

questions.explanation: Guaranteed forward movement is precisely what the time-of-day clock lacks.

questions.question: How do you use a monotonic clock value, and what is forbidden?

options.text: Read it twice and take the difference between the two values
You compare absolute values across machines to order events
You use the absolute value as a timestamp in stored data
You compare it against a time-of-day clock to detect drift

questions.explanation: Differences within a machine are meaningful; absolute values and cross-machine comparisons are not.

questions.question: What complication arises with multiple CPU sockets?

options.text: Separate timers per CPU socket, which the OS tries to hide
There is one timer shared by all sockets, so no complication arises
The operating system exposes each socket's timer separately
Multi-socket servers cannot provide a monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: The OS papers over it, imperfectly.

questions.question: What is slewing, and what can NTP do and not do to a monotonic clock?

options.text: NTP may slew the clock, changing how fast it moves forward
Slewing means jumping the clock; NTP can slew but not adjust frequency
NTP can jump the monotonic clock but not slew it
NTP cannot affect the monotonic clock at all

questions.explanation: 0.05% is 500 parts per million, which over an hour is about 1.8 seconds and over a day about 43.2 seconds.

questions.question: Why are monotonic clocks fine in distributed systems?

options.text: Because measuring elapsed time needs no cross-node synchronization
Because monotonic clocks are synchronized by NTP across nodes
Because their absolute values are comparable between machines
They are not fine at all; time-of-day clocks are preferred here

questions.explanation: Monotonic clocks don't need synchronization, but time-of-day clocks need to be set according to an NTP server or other external time source in order to be useful.

questions.question: Which properties belong to the monotonic clock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is meaningless to compare its values across machines
It can be slewed but never jumped by NTP
It is the right tool for measuring a service's response time
It counts seconds since a calendar epoch

questions.explanation: Counting from a calendar epoch, jumping backward, needing an external time source, and being right for a 'when was this published' field all belong to the time-of-day clock.

questions.question: What is clock drift, what figure does Google assume, and what does it imply?

options.text: It drifts, running fast or slow depending on temperature
Google assumes 2 ppm, giving 0.06 ms over 30 seconds
Google assumes 2000 ppm, giving 60 ms over 30 seconds
Clock drift is constant per machine regardless of temperature

questions.explanation: At 200 ppm, an hour of drift is about 0.72 seconds and a week is about 121 seconds — roughly two minutes.

questions.question: What happens when a computer's clock differs too much from its NTP server?

options.text: It refuses to synchronize, or the local clock is forcibly reset
It slews the clock gradually, with no visible jump at all
It raises an error that is reported to every application
It shuts the machine down to prevent data corruption

questions.explanation: A node can also be accidentally firewalled off from NTP servers, and the misconfiguration may go unnoticed for some time — anecdotal evidence suggests this does happen in practice.

questions.question: How accurate can NTP be over the internet, and how does it fail?

options.text: Because NTP accuracy is limited by the network delay
NTP is accurate to microseconds over the internet with no failure mode
NTP is accurate to 1 ms with spikes to 5 ms
NTP accuracy is independent of network delay

questions.explanation: The 35 ms minimum is about 350 times worse than the 100-microsecond MiFID II requirement, and the one-second spike is about 30 times worse again than the 35 ms floor.

questions.question: How wrong can NTP servers be, and why are clients nonetheless robust?

options.text: Some NTP servers report times that are off by hours
NTP servers are never wrong; clients trust a single server
NTP servers can be off by milliseconds at most
Clients ignore all servers and use the local clock

questions.explanation: The NTP client contacts all configured servers, estimates their errors, and checks that a majority of servers agree on some time range — so a misconfigured server is detected as an outlier and excluded from synchronization.

questions.question: What happens to clocks in virtual machines?

options.text: The hardware clock is virtualized, so it can jump
Virtual machines have perfectly accurate clocks provided by the hypervisor
Virtual machine clocks run backward during pauses
Virtualization has no effect on clocks

questions.explanation: The same phenomenon as the hypervisor-induced network queueing, seen through the clock.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about clocks on devices you don't control?

options.text: Because you cannot trust the hardware clock on a device you don't control
Mobile clocks are synchronized by the carrier and always correct
Embedded devices are fitted with atomic clocks as standard
Users have no way of changing a device's hardware clock

questions.explanation: Deliberate manipulation is the specific risk, not just drift.

questions.question: State the MiFID II clock requirement and its purposes.

options.text: Within 100 microseconds of UTC, under a draft European regulation
Within 100 milliseconds of UTC, to help with billing
Within 1 second of UTC, to help with audit logging
Within 1 microsecond of UTC, to help with order matching

questions.explanation: 100 microseconds is about 350 times tighter than the 35 ms minimum error seen when synchronizing over the internet, and about 70 times tighter than a few milliseconds on a local network.

questions.question: How is such accuracy achieved, and how does it break?

options.text: GPS receivers, the Precision Time Protocol, and careful monitoring
Through NTP alone, which does not fail when properly configured
Through an atomic clock in every machine, which cannot fail
It cannot be achieved at all with currently available hardware

questions.explanation: Achievable but expensive, and fragile in operation.

questions.question: True or false: a drifting clock usually announces itself by failing loudly; NTP can be more accurate than the network round-trip time; a misconfigured NTP server reporting a time off by hours will typically be ignored by clients; clock drift is a constant per machine.

options.text: False, false, true, false
True, true, true, true
False, true, false, true
True, false, true, false

questions.explanation: Only the outlier-rejection claim is true as stated.

questions.question: Why are broken clocks worse than broken CPUs?

options.text: Because a bad clock breaks data subtly instead of stopping the node
A broken clock crashes the machine, whereas a broken CPU does not
A broken clock is always caught immediately by monitoring
The two kinds of fault are equally noticeable in practice

questions.explanation: Silence is the danger: the fault does not announce itself.

questions.question: If your software requires synchronized clocks, what is essential?

options.text: Monitor the clock offsets between all the machines
It is essential to use only monotonic clocks
It is essential to disable NTP
No monitoring is needed at all, provided NTP has been configured

questions.explanation: Treat a drifting clock as a node failure.

questions.question: Walk through Figure 8-3's sequence of events.

options.text: A dangerous use of time-of-day clocks under multi-leader replication
It shows single-leader replication with a failover
It shows leaderless replication with quorum reads
It shows a partitioned database with cross-partition writes

questions.explanation: Multi-leader plus timestamp-tagged writes is the dangerous combination.

questions.question: What are the timestamps and the ordering error in Figure 8-3?

options.text: That the skew is under 3 ms, better than you can usually expect
The skew is 300 ms and the timestamp error is 100 ms
The timestamps are correctly ordered, so there is no error
The skew is 3 seconds and the timestamp error is 1 second

questions.explanation: Very good synchronization still inverts the order of causally related writes.

questions.question: What does node 2 do, and what is the outcome?

options.text: Because B's causally later write carries the earlier timestamp
Node 2 detects the inversion and raises an error to the client
Node 2 keeps both of the values as siblings for later merging
Node 2 discards the write x = 1 as a duplicate of the other

questions.explanation: This is the last write wins conflict resolution strategy, widely used in both multi-leader replication and leaderless databases such as Cassandra and Riak. Some implementations generate timestamps on the client rather than the server, but this doesn't change the fundamental problems with LWW.

questions.question: Which problems does the chapter name with last write wins? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Database writes can mysteriously disappear: a node with a lagging clock is unable to overwrite values previously written by a node with a fast clock until the clock skew between the nodes has elapsed, allowing arbitrary amounts of data to be silently dropped without any error being reported to the application

LWW cannot distinguish between writes that occurred sequentially in quick succession — where client B's increment definitely occurs after client A's write — and writes that were truly concurrent, where neither writer was aware of the other. Additional causality tracking mechanisms such as version vectors are needed to prevent violations of causality

It is possible for two nodes to independently generate writes with the same timestamp, especially when the clock only has millisecond resolution; an additional tiebreaker value — which can simply be a large random number — is required to resolve such conflicts, but this approach can also lead to violations of causality
Last-write-wins causes corruption of the data on disk

questions.explanation: Three problems: vanishing writes, conflated sequential and concurrent writes, and timestamp collisions.

questions.question: What illustration does the chapter give of residual skew even under tight NTP synchronization?

options.text: A packet appearing to arrive before it was sent
A packet arrives 100 ms after it was sent, which is expected
Two nodes report identical timestamps for different events
The clocks jump backward simultaneously

questions.explanation: An impossible ordering produced by a few milliseconds of residual skew.

questions.question: Could NTP be made accurate enough that incorrect orderings cannot occur?

options.text: Probably not, since NTP accuracy is bounded by round-trip time
Yes, because GPS receivers make NTP exact to the nanosecond
Yes, given sub-millisecond NTP on a quiet local network
The question is meaningless, since packets have no timestamps

questions.explanation: The measuring instrument is bounded by the very quantity it must resolve.

questions.question: Define logical clocks and contrast them with physical clocks.

options.text: Incrementing counters rather than a quartz oscillator
Logical clocks measure elapsed time more precisely than physical clocks
Logical clocks are synchronized by NTP
Logical and physical clocks are the same thing

questions.explanation: Ordering without magnitude is exactly what causality needs.

questions.question: Distinguish a clock's resolution from its accuracy, and give the accuracy figures.

options.text: Resolution is not the same thing as accuracy
Resolution equals accuracy in modern systems
Accuracy is always better than resolution
Accuracy on a local network is nanoseconds

questions.explanation: Fine resolution on an inaccurate reading is precision theatre.

questions.question: How do you compute the clock uncertainty bound? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you have a GPS receiver or atomic (caesium) clock directly attached to your computer, the expected error range is reported by the manufacturer

If you're getting the time from a server, the uncertainty is based upon the expected quartz drift since your last sync with the server, plus the NTP server's own uncertainty, plus the network round-trip time to the server — to a first approximation, and assuming you trust the server
It is exactly equal to the clock's reported resolution
It is always zero for a clock synchronized by NTP

questions.explanation: Most systems don't expose this uncertainty: when you ask for the time using clock_gettime() the return value doesn't tell you the expected error of the timestamp, so you don't know if its confidence interval is five milliseconds or five years.

questions.question: Describe Google's TrueTime API.

options.text: TrueTime in Spanner, which returns an explicit confidence interval
It returns a single exact timestamp guaranteed correct to the nanosecond
It returns a logical counter with no physical meaning
It returns the network round-trip time

questions.explanation: An interval rather than a point is the key design move.

questions.question: Why are distributed transaction IDs hard to generate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Coordination: a global, monotonically increasing transaction ID across all partitions is difficult to generate, because it requires coordination

Causality: the transaction ID must reflect causality — if transaction B reads a value that was written by transaction A, then B must have a higher transaction ID than A, otherwise the snapshot would not be consistent
With lots of small, rapid transactions, creating transaction IDs in a distributed system becomes an untenable bottleneck
Because transaction IDs are required to be globally unique strings

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that distributed sequence number generators do exist, such as Twitter's Snowflake, which generate approximately monotonically increasing unique IDs in a scalable way by allocating blocks of the ID space to different nodes — but they typically cannot guarantee an ordering that is consistent with causality, because the timescale at which blocks of IDs are assigned is longer than the timescale of database reads and writes.

questions.question: State the observation Spanner's snapshot isolation is based on.

options.text: If the intervals do not overlap, the order is definitely known
If the midpoints of the intervals differ, the order is determined
If the intervals overlap, the order is determined by node ID
Interval comparison never determines order

questions.explanation: Non-overlap gives a provable order; overlap gives none.

questions.question: What does Spanner deliberately do before committing, and what hardware makes it affordable?

options.text: It waits out the confidence interval before committing
It commits immediately and resolves conflicts later; no special hardware is needed
It waits one second per transaction, using NTP only
It uses logical clocks and no waiting

questions.explanation: A 7 ms commit wait bounds a single sequential committer to roughly 143 commits per second. The chapter notes that clock-based distributed transaction semantics is an area of active research — interesting, but not yet implemented in mainstream databases outside of Google.

questions.question: What problem opens 'Process Pauses', and how does a lease solve it?

options.text: How a node knows it is still the leader
The node asks all other nodes on every write; a lease caches the answer
The node checks its own clock; a lease adds a timestamp
There is no such problem, because leadership is permanent once granted

questions.explanation: A lock with a timeout, renewed while healthy.

questions.question: What is wrong with a request-handling loop that checks whether the lease has less than 10 seconds remaining before renewing?

options.text: On synchronized clocks, since the expiry was set by another machine
It renews far too often, which wastes network bandwidth
It uses a monotonic clock, which cannot measure an expiry time
Nothing is wrong with it, provided NTP is running everywhere

questions.explanation: Comparing a remotely-set time-of-day expiry against a local clock is the bug.

questions.question: How long can garbage collection pauses last, and what does the chapter say about 'concurrent' collectors?

options.text: Garbage collection, which stops all running threads
GC pauses last at most a few milliseconds; concurrent collectors never stop the world
GC pauses last seconds and can be eliminated by tuning
GC pauses do not affect distributed systems

questions.explanation: Several minutes is an order of magnitude larger than most lease durations.

questions.question: Which whole-machine suspension causes does the chapter describe? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In virtualized environments a virtual machine can be suspended, pausing the execution of all processes and saving the contents of memory to disk, and resumed — a pause that can occur at any time in a process's execution and can last for an arbitrary length of time
Live migration of virtual machines from one host to another without a reboot, where the length of the pause depends on the rate at which processes are writing to memory
On end-user devices such as laptops, execution may also be suspended and resumed arbitrarily, for example when the user closes the lid of their laptop
Network interface resets, which suspend the CPU while they run

questions.explanation: Three whole-machine causes, all invisible to the paused process.

questions.question: Describe the scheduling-related pauses and define steal time.

options.text: A context switch to another thread, or to another virtual machine
Steal time is CPU time consumed by the garbage collector
Steal time is the time lost to clock drift between nodes
A context switch cannot pause a thread partway through a function

questions.explanation: Arbitrary preemption points, with steal time as the virtualized variant.

questions.question: Describe the surprise disk I/O pause cause and its compounding factors.

options.text: Synchronous disk access, which can happen unexpectedly
Disk I/O only pauses threads that explicitly open files
Disk I/O pauses are bounded by the disk's seek time
Network storage eliminates I/O pauses

questions.explanation: Lazy classloading is the surprising trigger; network storage and GC are the compounding factors.

questions.question: Explain the swapping-related pause and define thrashing.

options.text: A page fault forcing a swap from disk
Thrashing means excessive garbage collection
Thrashing means excessive context switching
Paging never causes pauses on modern systems

questions.explanation: Disabling paging on servers is the standard operational response.

questions.question: Describe the signal-based pause and the general conclusion the chapter draws.

options.text: The SIGSTOP signal, as sent by Ctrl-Z in a shell
SIGSTOP terminates the process permanently
SIGSTOP is only available in virtualized environments
SIGSTOP pauses only I/O, not CPU

questions.explanation: The thread does not notice, which is exactly what makes these pauses dangerous.

questions.question: Why don't single-machine concurrency tools transfer to distributed systems?

options.text: Mutexes, semaphores, atomic counters and lock-free data structures
They transfer directly, since a distributed lock is just a mutex
They fail only because of clock skew between the machines
They fail only because of latency added by the network

questions.explanation: No shared memory is the structural reason; unnoticed pauses are the practical one.

questions.question: Define a hard real-time system, and what does the 'Is real-time really real?' box distinguish?

options.text: That the system meets specified timing guarantees in all circumstances
Real-time means high performance, and the two usages agree
Real-time means low latency, with no guarantee attached
The two usages are identical in meaning and in practice

questions.explanation: Guaranteed deadlines in all circumstances versus 'fast enough usually'.

questions.question: What does providing real-time guarantees require, and what does it cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Support from all levels of the software stack: a real-time operating system that allows processes to be scheduled with a guaranteed allocation of CPU time in specified intervals; library functions must document their worst-case execution times; dynamic memory allocation may be restricted or disallowed entirely (real-time garbage collectors exist, but the application must still ensure it doesn't give the GC too much work to do); and an enormous amount of testing and measurement must be done to ensure guarantees are met
All of this severely restricts the range of programming languages, libraries and tools that can be used, since most languages and tools do not provide real-time guarantees

Developing real-time systems is very expensive, and they are most commonly used in safety-critical embedded devices. Moreover, 'real-time' is not the same as 'high-performance': real-time systems may have lower throughput, since they have to prioritize timely responses above all else
For server-side data processing real-time guarantees are both economical and now standard practice

questions.explanation: The chapter says the opposite: for most server-side data processing systems real-time guarantees are simply not economical or appropriate, so those systems must live with pauses and clock instability. Everything required, and why server-side systems decline to pay for it.

questions.question: Which techniques does the chapter offer for limiting the impact of garbage collection?

options.text: Treat them as brief planned outages and route traffic elsewhere
Disable garbage collection entirely on the server nodes
Run a real-time operating system for all server workloads
Increase the heap size until garbage collection never runs

questions.explanation: Both emerging ideas rely on the runtime tracking the rate of object allocation and the remaining free memory over time so collections can be scheduled. The caveat: these measures cannot fully prevent garbage collection pauses, only reduce their impact on the application.

questions.question: Summarize how distributed systems differ from a single computer, and the limit on a node's knowledge.

options.text: No shared memory, only an unreliable network, with partial failures
Nodes share memory but not clocks, so only timing is uncertain
Nodes can determine each other's state by direct inspection
Only partial failure distinguishes distributed systems

questions.explanation: The chapter admits these discussions border on the philosophical, since our mechanisms for perception and measurement are unreliable — though in computing, unlike philosophy, we do expect the system to obey the laws we expect of the physical world, such as cause and effect.

questions.question: How does the chapter say we avoid 'figuring out the meaning of life'?

options.text: State the assumptions as a system model and design to meet them
By assuming the network is reliable and testing very thoroughly
By restricting yourself to single-node systems throughout
By accepting that reliable behaviour is simply unachievable

questions.explanation: State the model, design to it, prove within it.

questions.question: Describe the three funeral scenarios in 'The Truth Is Defined by the Majority'.

options.text: A node that receives every message but whose outgoing messages are dropped
Three scenarios about clock skew, network loss and disk corruption
Three scenarios about leader election, failover and split brain
Three scenarios about Byzantine nodes lying to each other

questions.explanation: The moral: a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment of a situation, so a distributed system cannot exclusively rely on a single node — otherwise, if that node fails, the system would be stuck and unable to recover.

questions.question: Which examples of 'only one of some thing' does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Only one node is allowed to be the leader for a database partition, to avoid split brain
Only one transaction or client is allowed to hold the lock for a particular resource or object, to prevent concurrently writing to it and corrupting it
Only one user is allowed to register a particular username, because a username must uniquely identify a user
Only one node in the cluster is allowed to hold a clock reading

questions.explanation: The trap: even if a node believes that it is 'the chosen one', that doesn't necessarily mean a quorum of nodes agrees. A node may have formerly been the leader, but if the other nodes declared it dead in the meantime due to a network interruption or GC pause, it may have been demoted and another leader may already have been elected — yet if it keeps acting as the chosen one and other nodes believe it, the system as a whole may do something incorrect.

questions.question: Walk through Figure 8-4, and which real system had this bug?

options.text: That only one client at a time may write the file
Two nodes both claim leadership and diverge; Cassandra had this bug
A clock jumps backward and writes are reordered; Riak had this bug
A network partition splits the cluster; ZooKeeper had this bug

questions.explanation: The figure's caption: incorrect implementation of a distributed lock, where client 1 believes that it still has a valid lease, even though it has expired, and thus corrupts a file in storage.

questions.question: Define a fencing token and walk through Figure 8-5 with its token numbers.

options.text: Every lock grant carries a monotonically increasing fencing token
A fencing token is a timestamp; the server rejects older timestamps
A fencing token is a client ID; the server accepts only the newest client
A fencing token is a checksum of the write

questions.explanation: The caption: making access to storage safe by allowing writes only in the order of increasing fencing tokens.

questions.question: Which ZooKeeper values can serve as fencing tokens, and where must the check happen?

options.text: The zxid transaction ID or the cversion node version
The session ID and the ephemeral node path; the client must check
The server timestamp and the watch counter; the lock service must check
ZooKeeper does not provide suitable tokens

questions.explanation: Some kind of check is necessary to avoid processing requests outside of the lock's protection, and the resource is the only place it can be enforced.

questions.question: What can fencing tokens not defend against, and what is the book's assumption about nodes?

options.text: A node acting in error, such as one whose lease has quietly expired
Fencing tokens defend against all faults, including malice
Fencing tokens defend only against clock skew between nodes
The book assumes nodes are adversarial by default throughout

questions.explanation: Reaching consensus in this untrusting environment is known as the Byzantine Generals Problem.

questions.question: Describe the Two Generals Problem.

options.text: Two generals who must agree but can only send unreliable messengers
Two generals must agree even though one of them is a traitor
Two generals share a radio channel that may be jammed
Two generals must synchronize their clocks before attacking

questions.explanation: Lost and delayed messengers, with no traitors — that is the non-Byzantine version.

questions.question: How does the Byzantine version differ?

options.text: n generals who must agree while some among them are traitors
There are exactly three generals, one of whom is known to be a traitor
All generals are traitors
The messengers are traitors rather than the generals

questions.explanation: Unknown identity of the traitors is what makes the problem hard.

questions.question: Where does the name 'Byzantine' come from?

options.text: An ancient Greek city, later Constantinople and now Istanbul
It refers to documented treachery among Byzantine generals
It refers to the Byzantine Empire's cryptographic systems
It was coined by Kyle Kingsbury

questions.explanation: The adjective, not the history, is the source.

questions.question: Define Byzantine fault-tolerant.

options.text: It keeps operating correctly even when nodes disobey the protocol
If it tolerates only malicious attackers, not malfunctioning nodes
If it tolerates only malfunctioning nodes, not attackers
If it tolerates network partitions

questions.explanation: Note both halves: the nodes need not be adversarial to be Byzantine — merely arbitrary.

questions.question: Why must flight control systems tolerate Byzantine faults?

options.text: Radiation corrupting memory or registers in aerospace systems
Because a pilot may deliberately issue a malicious command
Because flight software is written by untrusted outside vendors
Because air traffic control networks are publicly accessible

questions.explanation: Physics, not malice, produces arbitrary behaviour here.

questions.question: What is the second circumstance where Byzantine fault tolerance is relevant?

options.text: Multiple organizations, where some participants may try to defraud others
In single-organization datacenters, where insiders may be malicious
In web applications, where browsers are untrusted
In embedded systems, where hardware may be counterfeit

questions.explanation: Absence of a central authority among mutually untrusting parties is the defining condition.

questions.question: Why does this book assume no Byzantine faults? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Trust boundary: in your datacenter, all the nodes are controlled by your organization, so they can hopefully be trusted
Physics: cosmic radiation is fully blocked by datacenter roofing, so memory corruption simply cannot occur
Complexity: protocols for making systems Byzantine fault-tolerant are quite complicated, and fault-tolerant embedded systems rely on support from the hardware level
Cost: in most server-side data systems the cost of deploying Byzantine fault-tolerant solutions makes them impractical

questions.explanation: The chapter's physics point is weaker and more honest: radiation levels are low enough that memory corruption is not a major problem, not that it is impossible. Four reasons: trust, physics, complexity and cost.

questions.question: Which party must web applications expect arbitrary behaviour from, and what do they use instead of a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol?

options.text: Clients under end-user control, such as web browsers
Other servers in the same datacenter; they use Byzantine consensus
Database replicas; they use quorum voting
Network switches; they use checksums

questions.explanation: A central authority replaces Byzantine agreement whenever one exists.

questions.question: Why can't a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm save you from your own bugs?

options.text: Because the same buggy software on every node defeats the algorithm
Because a software bug is not a Byzantine fault by definition
Because Byzantine algorithms require unanimity among nodes
It can save you, provided that the bug is sufficiently rare

questions.explanation: With n = 4, more than two-thirds means more than 2.67 nodes correct, so at least 3 correct and therefore at most 1 faulty — and the same bug in the same code breaks all four.

questions.question: Could a protocol protect against vulnerabilities and compromise?

options.text: Because an attacker who compromises one node can likely compromise all
Yes — Byzantine fault tolerance solves the security problem completely
Yes, provided that fewer than one-third of the nodes are compromised
No, and there is no protection of any kind against this

questions.explanation: Homogeneity of software defeats the quorum assumption for attackers as well as for bugs.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by weak forms of lying, and how does it characterize the countermeasures?

options.text: Guards against weak forms of lying, short of full Byzantine tolerance
They constitute full Byzantine fault tolerance at a low cost
They defend successfully against a determined adversary
They are not worth implementing in any server-side system

questions.explanation: Pragmatic partial protection, honestly labelled as such.

questions.question: What does the chapter recommend about packet corruption?

options.text: Corrupted packets, usually but not always caught by checksums
TCP checksums are sufficient; no application-level check is needed
Full cryptographic signing is required on every packet
Packet corruption does not occur in modern networks

questions.explanation: Application-level checksums catch what TCP and UDP miss.

questions.question: What input checks does the chapter name, inside and outside the firewall?

options.text: Sanitize user input, checking ranges and limiting sizes
Public applications need no checks; internal ones need strict checks
Both need identical, maximally strict checks
Neither of them needs checking, provided the connection uses TLS

questions.explanation: Graduated strictness by trust boundary, but never zero.

questions.question: Describe NTP's majority check and the conclusion.

options.text: Configure several NTP servers and compare their estimates
The client uses only the first responding server
The client averages all servers including outliers
The client trusts the server with the lowest stratum number unconditionally

questions.explanation: This is the majority-agreement idea from The Truth Is Defined by the Majority, applied to time.

questions.question: Define a system model, and why do algorithms need one?

options.text: Not to depend too heavily on the specific hardware and software
A system model is a benchmark of the system's performance
A system model is a diagram of the deployment topology
A system model is the concrete implementation of an algorithm

questions.explanation: Formalizing expected faults is what allows correctness proofs — needed for problems like consensus in Chapter 9.

questions.question: State the synchronous model, the misreading it heads off, and the verdict on its realism.

options.text: Bounded network delay, bounded process pauses, and bounded clock error
It assumes zero delay and perfectly synchronized clocks, and is realistic
It assumes unbounded delay, and is the realistic choice
It assumes there are no clocks in the system at all

questions.explanation: Bounded, not zero — and still unrealistic.

questions.question: Define partial synchrony and give both halves of the argument for its realism.

options.text: Bounded most of the time, but sometimes exceeding those bounds
It means the delays are always large, but nonetheless bounded
It means clocks are synchronized even though networks are not
It is not a realistic model of any deployed system

questions.explanation: Note 'arbitrarily large', not 'large but bounded' — that distinction is what makes the model hard.

questions.question: What is an algorithm forbidden from doing in the asynchronous model?

options.text: No timing assumptions at all, and not even a clock
It cannot send messages at all, only receive them
It cannot make use of any persistent storage
It cannot assume that the other nodes are honest

questions.explanation: No clock means no timeouts, which rules out most practical failure detection.

questions.question: Match the timing models to their defining statements.

options.text: Synchronous has fixed bounds; partially synchronous exceeds them sometimes
Synchronous has no clock; asynchronous has bounded delay
Partially synchronous has no clock; synchronous is occasionally unbounded
All three assume bounded delay, differing only in clock accuracy

questions.explanation: The chapter calls the synchronous model not realistic, partial synchrony a realistic model of many systems, and the asynchronous model very restrictive.

questions.question: State the crash-stop assumption, including what makes it stop rather than merely crash.

options.text: That a node fails only by crashing and never comes back
The node crashes and recovers after a known delay
The node crashes and recovers with its memory intact
The node slows down but never stops

questions.explanation: 'Never comes back' is what distinguishes crash-stop from crash-recovery.

questions.question: Give the crash-recovery assumptions, being precise about state.

options.text: Nodes may crash and later recover, with stable storage surviving
In-memory state survives a crash while disk state is lost
Both in-memory and on-disk state survive a node crash
Both are lost, but the recovery time is known in advance

questions.explanation: Disk survives, memory does not, and the recovery time is unknown.

questions.question: State the Byzantine node model, and why does 'arbitrary' matter?

options.text: Nodes may do absolutely anything, including deceiving other nodes
Nodes are always adversarial, being controlled by an attacker
Nodes may only crash or slow down, never behave arbitrarily
Nodes may lie, but only about timing and never about data

questions.explanation: Arbitrary covers both malice and mere corruption.

questions.question: Of the nine combinations of timing and node models, which does the chapter single out?

options.text: Partially synchronous with crash-recovery faults
The synchronous model with crash-stop faults
The asynchronous model with Byzantine faults
The synchronous model with Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: Realistic timing plus realistic recovery behaviour, which is exactly what Chapter 9's algorithms target.
